title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
The page has two parts. The first is the end of §51. For the rod pinned at the ends and clamped at the midpoint L, the second family of modes satisfies tan(ω/2) = tanh(ω/2), which gives ω = 5π/2, 9π/2, …. Euler says the coefficients α, β, γ, δ follow exactly as in the earlier case five, except that sin(ω/2) ≠ 0 here.

The second part is Scholion §52, on a rod whose natural (unstressed) shape is an arbitrary curve EXF of arc length a. Euler proposes to take the curve itself as the axis. He uses the arc length s = EX and lets each point X move only along the normal XY to the curve, with y = XY. He then asserts three things:
- −y'' (with ' = d/ds) measures the excess of the deformed curvature at Y over the natural curvature at X.
- The equation of motion is therefore unchanged: (1/2g) y_tt = −b c² y_ssss.
- The regular modes keep the same form, y = C sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)) (α e^{s/f} + β e^{−s/f} + γ sin(s/f) + δ cos(s/f)) with f⁴ = b c² k.

Hence, he says, all the end-condition cases already treated (free, simply supported, clamped) and their tones carry over to curved rods without change. The only exception is a closed curve, which he takes up on the next page as the ring problem (§53, 'de sonis annulorum elasticorum'). In modern terms this is the claim that in-plane flexural vibration of a curved beam is governed by the straight Euler–Bernoulli beam equation written in arc length and normal displacement, so the frequencies would not depend on the curvature.
errors: The core claim of §52 is false. For a curved rod with natural curvature κ = 1/R, the change of curvature produced by a normal displacement w and a tangential displacement u is not −w''. It contains curvature terms: for a circle with inextensibility u' = w/R it is roughly w'' + w/R². Euler drops these terms.

The kinematic assumption that points move only along the normal is incompatible with inextensibility, which Euler assumes throughout via constant arc length. For a curved rod a purely normal motion stretches the axis. In reality normal and tangential motions are coupled, and the tangential inertia matters.

The consequence is that the stated frequencies are wrong for curved rods. For the ring (next page) this approach gives frequencies proportional to n⁴, with n the number of waves around the ring. The correct inextensional result (Hoppe 1871) is ω² ∝ n²(n²−1)²/(n²+1) · EI/(ρA R⁴). Euler's version even assigns a nonzero frequency to the n = 1 rigid translation.
For open curved rods with small curvature the error is of relative order (L/R)², so the claim works only as a shallow-curvature approximation, and Euler states no such limitation.

ideas.what: Second family of modes of the pinned-clamped-pinned rod via tan(ω/2) = tanh(ω/2), with coefficients as in case five
ideas.modern_name: Eigenmodes of a pinned–clamped beam segment
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E526); Daniel Bernoulli earlier for some beam cases

ideas.what: Reduction of the vibration of a naturally curved rod to the straight-rod equation, using arc length and normal displacement
ideas.modern_name: In-plane flexural vibration of curved beams and rings (erroneous shallow-curvature reduction)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler attempted it (also the 1764/66 bell paper E303); correct ring theory by R. Hoppe (1871), later Lamb, Rayleigh and Love
ideas.where_published: E526 §§52–53; cf. E303 'Tentamen de sono campanarum'; discussed by Truesdell, The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Interpreting −y'' as the excess of actual curvature over natural curvature (curvature-change constitutive law for a pre-curved rod)
ideas.modern_name: Bending moment proportional to the change of curvature in a naturally curved elastica
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, for the static case (De curvis elasticis 1744; later papers on naturally curved laminae)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I and later elastica papers

deep.surprise_reason: The page carries a known (and flawed) generalization to curved rods that leads into Euler's ring analysis. Truesdell already discusses Euler's treatment and its error, and Hoppe and Rayleigh supplied the correct theory. Nothing here appears absent from the historical record.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. The second exponential is e^{−s/f}, as the image shows a minus sign over the exponent.
